pos: n. (the pupil of the eye; also fruit; rendering Hebrew ishon, the little man)
etymology: Old English aeppel. The Hebrew idiom apple of the eye is literally the little man of the eye — the tiny reflection a person sees of himself in another's pupil.
biblical_def: Apple in Scripture most often means the pupil of the eye. Moses says God found Jacob in a waste howling wilderness and “kept him as the apple of his eye” (Deu 32:10). David prays, “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings” (Psa 17:8), and Zechariah warns that “he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye” (Zec 2:8). Proverbs uses the fruit: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apple as the fruit of the apple tree; and the pupil of the eye.
webster_full: APPLE, n. The fruit of the apple tree, from the genus Pyrus.
2. The pupil of the eye.
scriptures: He found him in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.
Psa 17:8
Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings,
Zec 2:8
For thus saith the LORD of hosts; After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
corruption_summary: God's care is imagined as broad benevolence, and the idiom Scripture chooses is the most reflexively protected square inch of the body.
corruption_paragraphs: The pupil is guarded by reflexes no one has to decide on — the eyelid closes before the mind registers the threat. That is the comparison Deuteronomy draws for God's keeping of Jacob: he kept him as the apple of his eye. Zechariah 2:8 turns it into a warning to the nations, since touching a man's pupil is the fastest way to provoke him.

The Hebrew adds a tenderness English loses. Ishon is a diminutive of man — the little man — named for the small figure you see reflected when you look closely into someone's eye. To be the apple of God's eye is to be the thing reflected when He looks.
roots_summary: Hebrew ishon (H380), the pupil, little man of the eye; bavah (H892), the gate or pupil, in Zechariah 2:8; tappuach (H8598), apple fruit.
roots_lines: Hebrew ishon (H380) — pupil, apple of the eye; Deuteronomy 32:10, Psalm 17:8, Proverbs 7:2.
Hebrew tappuach (H8598) — apple; Proverbs 25:11, Song of Solomon 2:3, 5.
usage: “He kept him as the apple of his eye” — guarded by reflex.
“He that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye” — a warning to the nations.
“Apples of gold in pictures of silver” — a word fitly spoken.

pos: n. (the years of being a child; rendering Hebrew yalduth)
etymology: Child with the ending -hood, a state or condition. Scripture treats childhood as a real season with its own vanity and its own opportunity.
biblical_def: Childhood is the season of being a child. Ecclesiastes closes its counsel to the young with it: “Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth… therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity” (Ecc 11:9–10), followed immediately by Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1). Paul reminds Timothy that “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines childhood as the state of a child, or the time in which persons are children, including the time from birth to puberty.
webster_full: CHILDHOOD, n. The state of a child, or the time in which persons are children, including the time from birth to puberty.
2. The properties of a child.
scriptures: Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.
Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Ecc 11:9

Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
corruption_summary: Childhood is treated as a rehearsal before real life, and Ecclesiastes calls it vanity in the sense of vapour — brief, real, and therefore urgent.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 11:9-12:1 refuses both the grim and the careless reading of youth. Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth — genuine permission — but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment. Then: childhood and youth are vanity. The Hebrew is hebel, vapour: not worthless, but brief. The urgency of Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth follows from the brevity, not from any contempt for the season.

2 Timothy 3:15 records what a childhood can carry: from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation. Timothy's grandmother and mother are named earlier in the letter. The instruction began before he could evaluate it and was still working decades later in a man Paul trusted with a church.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalduth (H3208), childhood, youth; hebel (H1892), vapour, vanity; Greek brephos (G1025), an infant — from a child in 2 Timothy 3:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalduth (H3208) — childhood, youth; Ecclesiastes 11:10, Psalm 110:3.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, vanity; the word behind childhood and youth are vanity.
Greek brephos (G1025) — infant, babe; 2 Timothy 3:15, Luke 18:15.
usage: “Childhood and youth are vanity” — vapour, and therefore urgent.
“Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth” — the conclusion drawn from brevity.
“From a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” — instruction that outlasted the instructors.

pos: v. (to utter the cock's cry; rendering Greek phoneo)
etymology: Old English crawan, imitative. In the Gospels the crowing of a cock is a clock, a prophecy, and a rebuke in one sound.
biblical_def: To crow is to utter the cock's cry. Christ times Peter's denial by it: “Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mat 26:34). Peter protests, and then “immediately the cock crew. And Peter remembered the word of Jesus” (Mat 26:74–75). John records the same exchange (Joh 13:38), and Mark notes the cock crowing twice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crow as to cry as a cock; to make the noise of a cock; and to boast in triumph, to vaunt.
webster_full: CROW, v.i. To cry as a cock.
2. To boast in triumph; to vaunt; to vapor; to swagger.
CROW, n. A large black fowl of the genus Corvus.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.
And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.
Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.
corruption_summary: Confidence in one's own loyalty is treated as evidence of it, and Peter's collapse was predicted to the hour by the One he was reassuring.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 26:33-35 records Peter's self-assessment twice, and it escalates: though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended… Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. He was not lying. He genuinely meant it, and he was genuinely wrong, which is the point. Sincerity is not the same as self-knowledge, and Christ's answer was not a rebuke but a timetable.

The mercy is in what the crowing produced: and Peter remembered the word of Jesus… and he went out, and wept bitterly. A bird's ordinary noise at dawn became the instrument of a man's restoration. Judas also failed that week and went out; the difference between the two is entirely in what happened after the failure.
roots_summary: Greek phoneo (G5455), to call out, to crow; alektor (G220), a cock — the two words always paired in the denial accounts.
roots_lines: Greek phoneo (G5455) — to crow, call; Matthew 26:34, 74-75, Luke 22:60-61.
Greek alektor (G220) — cock; the four Gospels' shared detail.
Greek alektorophonia (G219) — cockcrowing, a watch of the night; Mark 13:35.
usage: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” — a timetable, not a rebuke.
“Immediately the cock crew. And Peter remembered” — an ordinary noise doing mercy's work.
“He went out, and wept bitterly” — the difference from Judas.

pos: n. pl. (rhythmic movement in celebration; rendering Hebrew mecholah)
etymology: From Old French dancier. Scripture's dances are almost always women celebrating a deliverance, and one of them ends a life.
biblical_def: Dances are celebratory movement. Miriam leads them after the Red Sea: “all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances” (Exo 15:20). Jephthah's daughter meets him with timbrels and dances — and she was his only child (Jdg 11:34). Israel's women greet David with the song that set Saul against him (1Sa 18:6–7), and Jeremiah promises restoration: “thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry” (Jer 31:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dance as to leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument; and a leaping and frisking about.
webster_full: DANCE, v.i. To leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument.
2. To leap and frisk about; to move nimbly or up and down.
DANCE, n. A leaping or stepping with motions of the body adjusted to the measure of a tune.
scriptures: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.
And Jephthah came to Mizpeh unto his house, and, behold, his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances: and she was his only child; beside her he had neither son nor daughter.

And it came to pass as they came, when David was returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, that the women came out of all cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul, with tabrets, with joy, and with instruments of musick.
Jer 31:4
Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel: thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry.
corruption_summary: Celebration is treated as trivial beside doctrine, and Scripture stations dances at the Red Sea, at Goliath's defeat, and at the promise of Israel's return.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 11:34 is the cruellest sentence in the book because of where the dancing falls. Jephthah came to his house, and, behold, his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances: and she was his only child. She was celebrating a victory; he was returning under a rash vow. The narrative does not commend the vow, and the chapter stands as a permanent warning about bargaining with God in a moment of fear.

Jeremiah 31:4 puts dancing in the future tense as a promise to a nation in ruins: again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel: thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry. Restoration is described not merely as return but as the recovery of the capacity for joy, which is often the last thing to come back.
roots_summary: Hebrew mecholah (H4246), a dance; machol (H4234), dancing — from a root meaning to whirl; toph (H8596), a timbrel.
roots_lines: Hebrew mecholah (H4246) — dance; Exodus 15:20, Judges 11:34, 1 Samuel 18:6.
Hebrew machol (H4234) — dancing; Psalm 30:11, thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing.
Hebrew toph (H8596) — timbrel, tambourine; the constant companion instrument.
usage: “With timbrels and with dances” — Miriam at the sea.
“And she was his only child” — the dancing that met a rash vow.
“Shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry” — joy promised back.

pos: v. (killed by submersion; rendering Hebrew taba, Greek katapontizo)
etymology: Middle English drounen. Scripture's drownings are judgments, warnings, and one image of what money does to a soul.
biblical_def: Drowned means killed by water. Pharaoh's chosen captains “are drowned in the Red sea” (Exo 15:4), and Hebrews notes that the Egyptians assaying to pass through “were drowned” (Heb 11:29). Christ says of one who offends a little one, “it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea” (Mat 18:6). Paul says foolish and hurtful lusts “drown men in destruction and perdition” (1Ti 6:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines drown as to overwhelm in water; to overflow; to deluge; and to suffocate in water or other fluid.
webster_full: DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to overflow; to deluge; to inundate.
2. To deprive of life by immersion in water or other fluid.
3. To overwhelm; to immerse; to plunge and lose.
scriptures: Exo 15:4
Pharaoh's chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea.
By faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land: which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned.
Mat 18:6
But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
corruption_summary: Wealth is treated as a neutral tool, and Paul's image is of men going under — drowned in destruction and perdition by what they were chasing.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 6:9 is deliberately violent: they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. The subject is not the rich but they that will be rich — the wanting, not the having. And the verb is drowning, which is slow, involuntary at the end, and usually begins with someone confident they can swim.

Hebrews 11:29 makes a fine distinction about the same water: by faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land: which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned. The identical path, walked by two groups, with opposite outcomes. What separated them was not the route but faith — and the Egyptians' attempt is described with a word meaning to try, as if imitation of the outward act were enough.
roots_summary: Hebrew taba (H2883), to sink or drown; Greek katapontizo (G2670), to plunge into the sea; buthizo (G1036), to sink — the word in 1 Timothy 6:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew taba (H2883) — to sink, drown; Exodus 15:4, Jeremiah 38:6 of Jeremiah sinking in mire.
Greek katapontizo (G2670) — to drown, sink; Matthew 18:6, and 14:30 of Peter beginning to sink.
Greek buthizo (G1036) — to sink, drown; 1 Timothy 6:9, Luke 5:7.
usage: “His chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea” — judgment at the crossing.
“Which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned” — same path, opposite outcome.
“Which drown men in destruction” — the wanting, not the having.

pos: n. (a type or representation; rendering Greek tupos and parabole)
etymology: From Latin figura, a form. A figure in Scripture is a real thing that stands for another — the technical vocabulary of typology.
biblical_def: A figure is a type. Paul says Adam “is the figure of him that was to come” (Rom 5:14). Hebrews calls the tabernacle “a figure for the time then present” (Heb 9:9) and says Abraham received Isaac from the dead “in a figure” (Heb 11:19). Peter says baptism is the antitype that now saves us, “the like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us” (1Pe 3:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines figure as the form of any thing as expressed by the outline or terminating extremities; a representation; and in rhetoric, a mode of speaking or writing in which words are deflected from their ordinary signification.
webster_full: FIGURE, n. The form of any thing as expressed by the outline or terminating extremities.
2. Shape; form; person; as, a lady of elegant figure.
3. Distinguished appearance; eminence; distinction.
4. A statue; an image; that which is formed in resemblance of something else.
5. Representation in painting; the lines and colors which represent an animal.
scriptures: Rom 5:14
Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.
Heb 9:9
Which was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience;
Accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead; from whence also he received him in a figure.
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Typology is either abandoned as fanciful or extended without limit, and the New Testament supplies both the method and its boundaries by naming its own figures.
corruption_paragraphs: The safeguard against fanciful typology is that Scripture names its own figures. Adam is the figure of him that was to come, the tabernacle is a figure for the time then present, Isaac's return is in a figure, the flood prefigures baptism, the rock was Christ. Where the New Testament identifies a type, the reading is apostolic; where it does not, the interpreter is on his own and should say so.

Hebrews 9:9 also states the limitation of a figure: it was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience. A figure is by definition insufficient — it points because it cannot deliver. That is why the argument of Hebrews runs from shadow to substance rather than from good to better.
roots_summary: Greek tupos (G5179), a type, mark, pattern — from the impression a blow leaves; antitupon (G499), antitype; parabole (G3850), a figure or parable.
roots_lines: Greek tupos (G5179) — type, figure, print; Romans 5:14, John 20:25, the print of the nails.
Greek parabole (G3850) — figure, parable; Hebrews 9:9, 11:19.
Greek antitupon (G499) — antitype, like figure; 1 Peter 3:21, Hebrews 9:24.
usage: “Adam… is the figure of him that was to come” — typology named by an apostle.
“A figure for the time then present” — and it could not perfect the conscience.
“He received him in a figure” — Isaac given back from the dead.

pos: n. pl. (enemies; rendering Hebrew tsar, Greek echthros)
etymology: Old English fah, hostile. Foe is the sharper, older word for enemy — and Christ puts some of them at the family table.
biblical_def: Foes are enemies. Christ quotes Micah when describing the cost of following Him: “a man's foes shall be they of his own household” (Mat 10:36; Mic 7:6). The psalmist testifies, “When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell” (Psa 27:2). Acts applies the enthronement psalm to Christ: “until I make thy foes thy footstool” (Act 2:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foe as an enemy; one who entertains personal enmity, hatred, grudge or malice against another; and an enemy in war.
webster_full: FOE, n. An enemy; one who entertains personal enmity, hatred, grudge or malice, against another.
2. An enemy in war; a hostile army.
3. An opponent; an enemy; one who opposes any thing in principle.
scriptures: And a man's foes shall be they of his own household.
Mic 7:6
For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.
Psa 27:2
When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell.
Act 2:35
Until I make thy foes thy footstool.
corruption_summary: Following Christ is sold as improving every relationship, and He warned specifically that it would divide some households down the middle.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 10:34-36 is the passage least likely to appear on a promotional card: think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I am come to set a man at variance against his father… and a man's foes shall be they of his own household. Christ is not describing a failure of discipleship but a predictable consequence of it, and He says it so that converts from divided homes will not conclude they have done something wrong.

The comfort follows in the next verses rather than in a denial. He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me — and then, he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it. The cost is stated at full price, and the compensation is stated in the same breath. Micah, whom He quotes, ends the same passage with therefore I will look unto the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsar (H6862), adversary, foe; oyeb (H341), enemy; Greek echthros (G2190), hostile, an enemy.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsar (H6862) — adversary, foe; Psalm 27:2, 44:5, 60:12.
Greek echthros (G2190) — enemy, foe; Matthew 10:36, Acts 2:35, Romans 5:10.
Hebrew oyeb (H341) — enemy; Micah 7:6 in context, Psalm 110:1.
usage: “A man's foes shall be they of his own household” — a warning, not a failure.
“They stumbled and fell” — the psalmist's report of the outcome.
“Until I make thy foes thy footstool” — the enthronement psalm applied to Christ.

pos: n. (perverse contrariness; rendering Hebrew tahpukah)
etymology: From froward, literally turned away — the opposite of toward. Frowardness is a settled bent away from what is right.
biblical_def: Frowardness is perverse contrariness. Proverbs uses it of a disposition that enjoys wrong: those “who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked” (Pro 2:14). It marks the man who “deviseth mischief continually” and has “frowardness… in his heart” (Pro 6:14). The froward mouth is what the LORD hates (Pro 8:13), and wisdom's words have “nothing froward or perverse in them” (Pro 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frowardness as perverseness; a disposition to be contrary or disobedient; and untowardness.
webster_full: FROWARDNESS, n. Perverseness; a disposition to thwart or contradict; untowardness.
FROWARD, a. Perverse, that is, turning from, with aversion or reluctance; not willing to yield or comply with what is required; ungovernable; peevish.
scriptures: Pro 2:14
Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked;
Pro 6:14
Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord.
Pro 8:13
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
Pro 8:8
All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them.
corruption_summary: Contrariness is presented as independent thinking, and Proverbs describes a settled bent that turns from good the way a compass turns from a magnet.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 2:14 identifies frowardness by what it enjoys rather than by what it does: who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked. The tell is delight. A man may do wrong through weakness, ignorance, or pressure, and be recoverable; the froward take pleasure in the contrariness itself. That is a deeper problem than any single act, and it is what makes the froward so difficult to correct.

Proverbs 8:8 gives wisdom's opposite character: all the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them. Wisdom is entirely straight — nothing in it needs decoding for hidden angles, and nothing in it is designed to score against anyone. That is worth measuring one's own speech against, since a great deal of clever talk fails this test while sounding wise.
roots_summary: Hebrew tahpukah (H8419), perversity, frowardness, from a root meaning to overturn; iqqesh (H6141), crooked, perverse.
roots_lines: Hebrew tahpukah (H8419) — frowardness, perversity; Proverbs 2:12, 14, 6:14, 8:13.
Hebrew iqqesh (H6141) — crooked, froward; Proverbs 11:20, Psalm 101:4.
Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to overturn, turn; the root behind tahpukah.
usage: “Delight in the frowardness of the wicked” — identified by what it enjoys.
“Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually” — a settled bent.
“There is nothing froward or perverse in them” — wisdom is entirely straight.

pos: n. (a shaped mass of bread; rendering Greek artos)
etymology: Old English hlaf, bread. A loaf is bread in its whole form — and the disciples once crossed a lake worrying about having only one.
biblical_def: A loaf is a shaped bread. Mark records a moment of remarkable slowness: “now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, neither had they in the ship with them more than one loaf” (Mar 8:14) — and Christ, having just fed thousands twice, asks them, “Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?” (Mar 8:18). David distributes to all Israel “a loaf of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine” (1Ch 16:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loaf as a mass of bread when baked; and a mass or lump, as of sugar.
webster_full: LOAF, n. A mass of bread when baked. It is larger than a cake.
2. A mass or lump, as of sugar.
scriptures: Mar 8:14
Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, neither had they in the ship with them more than one loaf.
Mar 8:18
Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?
And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine.
Mar 8:21
And he said unto them, How is it that ye do not understand?
corruption_summary: Past provision is forgotten under present pressure, and the disciples counted one loaf in a boat with the Man who had fed nine thousand people.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 8:14-21 is almost comic and entirely convicting. They had one loaf and were reasoning among themselves because they had no bread. Christ works through the arithmetic with them — five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets? Twelve. Seven among four thousand? Seven. And then: how is it that ye do not understand? The problem was not information. They had gathered the leftovers themselves.

The relevant question is not whether God can provide but whether we remember that He has. Anxiety is very often a memory failure rather than a faith failure, which is why so much of Scripture is command to remember — and why the Supper Christ instituted is a meal of bread taken in remembrance.
roots_summary: Greek artos (G740), bread, a loaf; Hebrew kikkar lechem (H3603/H3899), a round loaf of bread.
roots_lines: Greek artos (G740) — bread, loaf; Mark 8:14, Matthew 14:17, John 6:9.
Hebrew kikkar (H3603) — a round, a loaf; 1 Chronicles 16:3, Judges 8:5.
Greek klasma (G2801) — fragment; the baskets of leftovers they had carried themselves.
usage: “Neither had they… more than one loaf” — counted in the presence of the Provider.
“Do ye not remember?” — anxiety as a memory failure.
“How is it that ye do not understand?” — the question left hanging.

pos: n. (a small liquid measure; rendering Hebrew log)
etymology: A transliteration of the Hebrew log, the smallest liquid measure named in Scripture — roughly half a pint.
biblical_def: A log is the smallest liquid measure in the law, and it appears only in the cleansing of the leper: the man brings two lambs, flour, “and one log of oil” (Lev 14:10). The priest pours it into his own left hand, dips his right finger, sprinkles seven times before the LORD, and puts the oil upon the tip of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the great toe of the right foot of him that is to be cleansed (Lev 14:15–17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines log as a Hebrew measure of liquids, containing, according to some authors, three quarters of a pint; according to others, five sixths of a pint.
webster_full: LOG, n. A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing, according to some authors, three quarters of a pint; according to others, five sixths of a pint.
LOG, n. A bulky piece or stick of timber unhewed.
scriptures: And on the eighth day he shall take two he lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb of the first year without blemish, and three tenth deals of fine flour for a meat offering, mingled with oil, and one log of oil. of
And the priest shall take some of the log of oil, and pour it into the palm of his own left hand:

And of the rest of the oil that is in his hand shall the priest put upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot, upon the blood of the trespass offering:

And if he be poor, and cannot get so much; then he shall take one lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, to make an atonement for him, and one tenth deal of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering, and a log of oil;
corruption_summary: Small quantities are assumed to be unimportant, and the law specifies half a pint of oil and exactly where each drop of it goes.
corruption_paragraphs: The leper's cleansing is one of the most detailed rituals in Leviticus, and the log of oil is applied with unusual precision: on the tip of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the great toe of the right foot — the same three points that were consecrated on Aaron and his sons at their ordination. The cleansed leper is marked exactly like a priest. What he hears, what he handles, and where he walks are all claimed.

Verse 21 makes provision that keeps the ritual from becoming a wealth test: and if he be poor, and cannot get so much, then he shall take one lamb… and a log of oil. The lambs may be reduced and the flour lessened, but the log of oil is not negotiable. The cheapest element in the ceremony is the one every cleansed man must bring in full.
roots_summary: Hebrew log (H3849), a liquid measure — occurring only in Leviticus 14, five times, all of oil.
roots_lines: Hebrew log (H3849) — a log measure; Leviticus 14:10, 12, 15, 21, 24.
Hebrew shemen (H8081) — oil; the substance measured.
Leviticus 8:23-24 uses the same three points — ear, thumb, toe — in the priests' consecration.
usage: “And one log of oil” — half a pint, specified.
“Upon the tip of the right ear… the thumb… the great toe” — marked like a priest.
“If he be poor… and a log of oil” — the one element never reduced.

pos: n. (working, active power; rendering Hebrew maaseh, Greek energeia)
etymology: From Latin operari, to work. An operation is God's working — the Greek gives us energy.
biblical_def: An operation is a working. Isaiah pronounces woe on those who “regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands” (Isa 5:12). Paul distinguishes gifts, administrations, and operations: “there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all” (1Co 12:6). Colossians says believers are risen with Christ “through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead” (Col 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines operation as the act or process of operating; agency; the exertion of power, physical, mechanical or moral; and action, effect.
webster_full: OPERATION, n. The act or process of operating; agency; the exertion of power, physical, mechanical or moral.
2. Action; effect.
3. Process; manipulation; series of acts in experiments.
4. In surgery, any methodical action of the hand on the human body.
scriptures: Isa 5:12
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.
And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all.
Col 2:12
Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.
Psa 28:5
Because they regard not the works of the LORD, nor the operation of his hands, he shall destroy them, and not build them up.
corruption_summary: God's activity is assumed to be visible only in the extraordinary, and Isaiah's woe falls on people too entertained to notice the operation of His hands.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 5:12 lists what occupied them instead: the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands. Nothing on the list is sinful. The charge is inattention — a life so continuously furnished with pleasant noise that the working of God passes unremarked. Psalm 28:5 attaches a consequence: because they regard not the works of the LORD… he shall destroy them, and not build them up.

1 Corinthians 12:6 is the reassuring counterpart for a congregation comparing itself: there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. The variety is real and it is deliberate; the source is single. Whatever a member is doing that is genuinely of God is God's own working, which makes both envy and contempt category errors.
roots_summary: Hebrew maaseh (H4639), a work or deed; Greek energeia (G1753), operative power; energema (G1755), an effect worked.
roots_lines: Hebrew maaseh (H4639) — work, operation; Isaiah 5:12, Psalm 28:5.
Greek energema (G1755) — operation, effect; 1 Corinthians 12:6, 10.
Greek energeia (G1753) — working, energy; Colossians 2:12, Ephesians 1:19, 3:7.
usage: “Neither consider the operation of his hands” — woe pronounced on inattention.
“Diversities of operations, but it is the same God” — variety with one source.
“Through the faith of the operation of God” — resurrection power applied.

pos: n. (a wind instrument; rendering Hebrew chalil, Greek aulos)
etymology: From Latin pipare, to chirp. The pipe is Scripture's instrument of both processional joy and funeral mourning.
biblical_def: A pipe is a wind instrument. Samuel meets a company of prophets coming down from the high place “with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp” (1Sa 10:5). Isaiah pictures pilgrims going up to the mountain of the LORD “as when one goeth with a pipe” (Isa 30:29). Christ likens His generation to children calling, “We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced” (Mat 11:17), and Paul asks how the pipe or harp shall be known without distinction in the sounds (1Co 14:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pipe as a wind instrument of music, made of reeds, straw, or wood; and a tube of clay, metal or other material.
webster_full: PIPE, n. A wind instrument of music, made of reeds, straw, or wood.
2. A long tube or hollow body.
3. A tube of clay used in smoking tobacco.
4. The organs of voice and respiration; as in windpipe.
scriptures: After that thou shalt come to the hill of God, where is the garrison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city, that thou shalt meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy:
Ye shall have a song, as in the night when a holy solemnity is kept; and gladness of heart, as when one goeth with a pipe to come into the mountain of the LORD, to the mighty One of Israel.
And saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented.
And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped?
corruption_summary: Worship music is argued about as taste, and Paul's concern is intelligibility — a pipe giving an uncertain sound teaches nobody anything.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:7 makes an argument from music that applies well past music: even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? Paul's subject is unintelligible tongues in the assembly, and his standard is whether the hearer can tell what is being said. Beauty is not the test; clarity is. A great deal of church practice would be reordered by that single criterion.

Matthew 11:17 uses the pipe for a generation that would respond to nothing: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented. Both the joyful tune and the funeral dirge were offered and both refused. Christ's diagnosis is that the objection was never really about John's fasting or His own eating.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalil (H2485), a pipe or flute, from a root meaning to bore; Greek aulos (G836), a flute; auleo (G832), to pipe.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalil (H2485) — pipe, flute; 1 Samuel 10:5, Isaiah 5:12, 30:29, 1 Kings 1:40.
Greek aulos (G836) — pipe, flute; only 1 Corinthians 14:7.
Greek auleo (G832) — to play the flute; Matthew 11:17, Luke 7:32.
usage: “A psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp” — the prophets coming down.
“We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced” — both tunes refused.
“Except they give a distinction in the sounds” — clarity as the standard.

pos: n., v. (a crowd; to push forward; rendering Greek ochlos and dioko)
etymology: From Latin pressare, to squeeze. In the Gospels the press is the crowd itself — the thing that has to be got through to reach Christ.
biblical_def: The press is a crowd, and to press is to push. Four men cannot bring their paralysed friend to Christ “for the press” and uncover the roof instead (Mar 2:4). Zacchaeus, being little of stature, “could not for the press” and climbs a sycomore (Luk 19:3). The woman with the issue of blood comes “in the press behind, and touched his garment” (Mar 5:27). Paul uses the verb of himself: “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Php 3:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines press as to urge with force or weight; to crowd; to throng; and as a noun, a crowd, a throng, a multitude of individuals crowded together.
webster_full: PRESS, v.t. To urge with force or weight; a word of extensive use, denoting the application of any power, physical or moral, to something that is to be moved or affected.
2. To squeeze; to crush; as, to press grapes.
PRESS, n. A crowd; a throng; a multitude of individuals crowded together.
scriptures: Mar 2:4
And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press, they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay.
Luk 19:3
And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.
Mar 5:27
When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment.
Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Obstacles to reaching Christ are treated as providence saying no, and three Gospel stories turn on people who refused to accept the crowd as an answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Three times the press stands between someone and Christ, and three times somebody does something undignified about it. Four friends dismantle a roof over a stranger's head. A chief tax collector, a wealthy adult, climbs a tree. An unclean woman pushes through a crowd she had no legal right to be in. In each case Christ responds to what the obstacle produced — when Jesus saw their faith; make haste, and come down; thy faith hath made thee whole.

Philippians 3:14 turns the same verb inward: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. Paul had just said he had not attained. Pressing is what a man does who is not there yet and has decided that not being there yet is not a reason to stop. The word carries effort and resistance in it, which is why it is the honest verb for the Christian life.
roots_summary: Greek ochlos (G3793), a crowd, press; dioko (G1377), to pursue, press toward; thlibo (G2346), to press or throng.
roots_lines: Greek ochlos (G3793) — crowd, press; Mark 2:4, 5:27, Luke 19:3.
Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, press toward; Philippians 3:12, 14.
Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, afflict; Mark 3:9, lest they should throng him.
usage: “They could not come nigh unto him for the press” — and they opened the roof.
“Could not for the press, because he was little of stature” — so he ran and climbed.
“I press toward the mark” — the honest verb for a man not yet arrived.

pos: n. pl. (raiders, plunderers; rendering Hebrew shasah)
etymology: From Latin spoliare, to strip. A spoiler strips a defeated people of goods — and in Judges God is said to deliver Israel into their hands.
biblical_def: Spoilers are plunderers. Judges records the cycle plainly: “the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them” (Jdg 2:14). The Philistines send out three companies of spoilers against Israel when there was no smith in the land (1Sa 13:17). Jeremiah announces that “the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon” (Jer 51:56), and Job notes that “the tabernacles of robbers prosper” for a season (Job 12:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spoiler as one who spoils; a plunderer; a pillager; a robber; and one who mars or corrupts any thing.
webster_full: SPOILER, n. One who spoils; a plunderer; a pillager; a robber.
2. One who mars or corrupts any thing.
SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to rob.
scriptures: Jdg 2:14

And the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about, so that they could not any longer stand before their enemies.
And the spoilers came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies: one company turned unto the way that leadeth to Ophrah, unto the land of Shual:
Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite.
Job 12:6
The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure; into whose hand God bringeth abundantly.
corruption_summary: Judgment is imagined as an event God sends, and Judges describes it as God handing a people over to the consequences already surrounding them.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 2:14 states the mechanism of the book's whole cycle: he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about. The enemies were already there; what changed was that God stopped restraining them. That is a sobering description of how national judgment usually arrives — not by a new catastrophe but by the withdrawal of a protection nobody had noticed was operating.

Job 12:6 records the observation that troubles every believer at some point: the tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure. Job says it in the middle of an argument, and he is not corrected for saying it. Scripture permits the observation. What it disputes is the conclusion — Jeremiah's answer being that the spoiler is himself eventually spoiled.
roots_summary: Hebrew shasah (H8154), to plunder, spoil; shadad (H7703), to deal violently, devastate — the spoiler of Jeremiah and Isaiah.
roots_lines: Hebrew shasah (H8154) — to spoil, plunder; Judges 2:14, 16, 1 Samuel 14:48.
Hebrew shadad (H7703) — to devastate, spoil; Jeremiah 51:56, Isaiah 33:1, woe to thee that spoilest.
Hebrew mashchith (H4889) — destroyer; 1 Samuel 13:17, the spoilers came out in three companies.
usage: “He delivered them into the hands of spoilers” — restraint withdrawn.
“The spoilers came out… in three companies” — against a nation with no smith.
“The tabernacles of robbers prosper” — the observation Scripture permits.

pos: v. part. (struck; also advanced in years; rendering Hebrew bo bayyamim, Greek probaino)
etymology: An older past participle of strike. The KJV uses it both for being struck and, in the idiom stricken in years, for being far advanced in age.
biblical_def: Stricken means struck, and in the age idiom, far advanced. Isaiah's Servant is stricken: “we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” (Isa 53:4). The age idiom appears often: Abraham and Sarah “were old and well stricken in age” (Gen 18:11); the LORD tells Joshua, “Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed” (Jos 13:1); and Zacharias and Elisabeth were “both now well stricken in years” (Luk 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stricken as struck; smitten; and advanced, as in stricken in years, far advanced in age.
webster_full: STRICKEN, pp. of strike. Struck; smitten.
2. Advanced; worn; far gone; as stricken in years.
scriptures: Isa 53:4
Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
Jos 13:1
Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed.
Now Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age; and it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women.
Luk 1:7
And they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years.
corruption_summary: Age is treated as the end of usefulness, and God's word to a man old and stricken in years was that much land remained to be possessed.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 13:1 is a striking thing for God to say to an old man: thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed. The observation about his age is accurate and is not offered as an excuse. The unfinished work is named in the same breath. Joshua spends the following chapters allotting territory he will never conquer himself, which is its own kind of faithfulness.

Isaiah 53:4 uses the other sense and records a misreading: we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. The crowd's inference was half right — He was indeed smitten of God — and entirely wrong about the cause. They assumed the sufferer deserved it. Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows corrects the account without denying the blow.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagah and nakah (H5221), to strike; the idiom ba bayyamim, come into days, for advanced age; Greek probaino (G4260), to go forward in years.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to strike, smite; Isaiah 53:4 in context.
Hebrew ba bayyamim — come into days; Genesis 18:11, Joshua 13:1, 23:1.
Greek probaino (G4260) — to advance; Luke 1:7, 18, well stricken in years.
usage: “We did esteem him stricken, smitten of God” — half right, entirely wrong.
“Thou art old… and there remaineth yet very much land” — no excuse offered.
“Both now well stricken in years” — and then Gabriel arrived.

pos: n. (a nursing infant; rendering Hebrew yonek, Greek thelazo)
etymology: From suck with the diminutive ending. A suckling is a child still at the breast — the least able person in any society.
biblical_def: A suckling is a nursing infant. The psalmist makes them God's chosen instrument: “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies” (Psa 8:2), which Christ quotes when children cry Hosanna in the temple and the chief priests object (Mat 21:16). Lamentations records the siege's cost: “the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city” (Lam 2:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suckling as a young child or animal nursed at the breast.
webster_full: SUCKLING, n. A young child or animal nursed at the breast.
2. A sort of white clover.
scriptures: Psa 8:2
Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.
And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?
Lam 2:11

Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
corruption_summary: Strength is assumed to require capacity, and Psalm 8 says God ordained strength out of the mouths of people who cannot yet speak.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 8:2 is a deliberate paradox: out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger. The least articulate members of the human race are named as God's answer to His adversaries. Christ quotes it in the temple against the chief priests who were offended by children shouting — and He quotes it as though the matter were settled by the psalm.

Lamentations 2:11 shows the other side, and Jeremiah does not spare his readers: mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled… because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city. The prophet who announced the judgment weeps over its cost to the smallest. Warning and grief are not alternatives in Scripture; the same man does both.
roots_summary: Hebrew yonek (H3243), a suckling; olel (H5768), a young child; Greek thelazo (G2337), to suckle.
roots_lines: Hebrew yonek (H3243) — suckling, nursing child; Psalm 8:2, Lamentations 2:11, 1 Samuel 15:3.
Greek thelazo (G2337) — to suck, nurse; Matthew 21:16, Luke 11:27.
Hebrew olel (H5768) — babe, little child; the companion word in Psalm 8:2.
usage: “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength” — God's chosen instrument.
“Have ye never read…?” — Christ settling the matter with the psalm.
“The children and the sucklings swoon in the streets” — the prophet weeping over his own message.

pos: adj. (wanting strength; rendering Greek asthenes)
etymology: From Old Norse veikr, pliant. Weakness in Scripture is a condition God repeatedly selects rather than merely tolerates.
biblical_def: Weak means wanting strength. Paul reports Christ's answer and his own conclusion: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness… for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2Co 12:9–10). Christ says in Gethsemane, “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41). Paul commands, “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1), and notes that God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty (1Co 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines weak as having little physical strength; feeble; infirm; not able to bear a great weight; and wanting spirit, wanting vigor of mind.
webster_full: WEAK, a. Having little physical strength; feeble.
2. Infirm; not healthy; as a weak constitution.
3. Not able to bear a great weight.
4. Low; small; as a weak voice.
5. Feeble of mind; wanting spirit; wanting vigor of understanding.
scriptures: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
corruption_summary: Weakness is hidden as a liability, and Paul advertises his — most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 12:9 records an answered prayer that did not remove the problem. Paul asked three times for the thorn to depart; the reply was my grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. He then does something almost nobody does with a limitation: most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. The thorn stayed, the interpretation changed, and the change was the answer.

Romans 14:1 turns the word toward the congregation with unusual care: him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations. The weaker brother is to be received — not tolerated at a distance, and not enrolled immediately in an argument about his scruples. Paul's entire chapter assumes the strong will be tempted to despise and the weak to judge, and forbids both.
roots_summary: Greek asthenes (G772), without strength, weak; astheneia (G769), infirmity; adunatos (G102), powerless.
roots_lines: Greek asthenes (G772) — weak, feeble; 2 Corinthians 12:10, Matthew 26:41, 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Greek astheneia (G769) — infirmity, weakness; 2 Corinthians 12:9, Hebrews 4:15.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to perfect, complete; my strength is made perfect in weakness.
usage: “When I am weak, then am I strong” — the interpretation changed, not the thorn.
“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” — said with sympathy, in a garden.
“Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” — received, not merely tolerated.

pos: v. (to rub clean or dry; rendering Hebrew machah, Greek exaleipho)
etymology: Old English wipian. Scripture's wiping runs from a dish scoured out in judgment to tears removed by God's own hand.
biblical_def: To wipe is to rub clean. God's judgment on Jerusalem uses a domestic image: “I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down” (2Ki 21:13). The promise reverses it: “he will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces” (Isa 25:8), repeated twice in Revelation — “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes” (Rev 7:17; 21:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wipe as to rub with something soft for cleaning; to clean by rubbing; and to strike off gently, to efface, to obliterate.
webster_full: WIPE, v.t. To rub with something soft for cleaning; to clean by rubbing; as, to wipe the hands or face with a towel.
2. To strike off gently.
3. To efface; to obliterate; to remove.
4. To cheat; to defraud.
scriptures: And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
Isa 25:8
He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it.
Rev 7:17
For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.
Rev 21:4
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
corruption_summary: Heaven is described as a place without sorrow, and Scripture describes something more personal — God's own hand removing tears from particular faces.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 21:4 is worded with unusual intimacy: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. Not the tears will cease, not sorrow will be forgotten — a hand goes to a face. The verse assumes there are tears there to be wiped, which means the grief carried into that moment is not denied or minimized on arrival. It is attended to, personally, by God.

2 Kings 21:13 uses the same verb for the opposite work: I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down. The picture is thorough and domestic — a dish scoured out and inverted so nothing remains in it. Set beside Revelation, the two uses show the range of the same hand: what it does to a city under judgment, and what it does to a face in glory.
roots_summary: Hebrew machah (H4229), to wipe, blot out; Greek exaleipho (G1813), to wipe away, obliterate — also used of blotting out sins.
roots_lines: Hebrew machah (H4229) — to wipe, blot out; 2 Kings 21:13, Isaiah 25:8, Genesis 6:7.
Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe away, blot out; Revelation 7:17, 21:4, Acts 3:19, Colossians 2:14.
Greek dakruon (G1144) — tear; the object of the wiping.
usage: “As a man wipeth a dish… turning it upside down” — judgment made domestic.
“The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces” — Isaiah's promise.
“God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes” — a hand to a face.

pos: adv. (plainly, distinctly; rendering Greek telaugos and kathorao)
etymology: From clear, Latin clarus, bright. Clearly in Scripture describes both restored eyesight and knowledge that cannot be pleaded ignorant of.
biblical_def: Clearly means plainly. Mark records a two-stage healing: after the second touch the blind man “was restored, and saw every man clearly” (Mar 8:25). Paul says the invisible things of God from the creation of the world “are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made… so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). Christ says to remove the beam from one's own eye, “and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye” (Mat 7:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clearly as plainly; evidently; fully; without obscurity; and without entanglement or confusion.
webster_full: CLEARLY, adv. Plainly; evidently; fully; as, the fact is clearly proved.
2. Without obstruction; luminously.
3. With clear discernment.
4. Without entanglement or confusion.
scriptures: Mar 8:25
After that he put his hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up: and he was restored, and saw every man clearly.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Mat 7:5
Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.
Mar 8:24
And he looked up, and said, I see men as trees, walking.
corruption_summary: Partial sight is mistaken for full sight, and Mark records a man who saw men as trees walking and needed a second touch.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 8:22-25 is the only two-stage miracle in the Gospels, and the middle stage is the instructive part: I see men as trees, walking. He was no longer blind and he was not yet seeing. Christ put his hands on him again, and he saw every man clearly. That intermediate condition — genuine sight, genuinely inadequate — describes a great deal of Christian understanding, and the remedy is another touch rather than a firmer resolve to squint.

Romans 1:20 removes the defence of ignorance about God's existence: the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse. Clearly is doing legal work in that sentence. The evidence is not obscure, which is why the verdict in the next verses concerns suppression rather than absence of light.
roots_summary: Greek telaugos (G5081), clearly, at a distance; kathorao (G2529), to see clearly; diablepo (G1227), to see through, in Matthew 7:5.
roots_lines: Greek telaugos (G5081) — clearly, plainly; only Mark 8:25.
Greek kathorao (G2529) — to see clearly, perceive; only Romans 1:20.
Greek diablepo (G1227) — to see clearly through; Matthew 7:5, Luke 6:42.
usage: “I see men as trees, walking” — genuine sight, genuinely inadequate.
“Clearly seen… so that they are without excuse” — the evidence is not obscure.
“Then shalt thou see clearly” — after the beam, not before.

pos: adv. (toward what is below; rendering Hebrew mattah)
etymology: Down with the directional ending. Scripture uses downward for roots, for the spirit of a beast, and for a remnant's growth.
biblical_def: Downward means toward what is below. Isaiah's promise to Hezekiah uses it of a remnant: “the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward” (Isa 37:31). Ecclesiastes asks who knows “the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth” (Ecc 3:21). Ezekiel measures the man of fire “from his loins even downward… the appearance of fire” (Eze 8:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines downward as from a higher place to a lower; in a descending course; and from a former time, or from an ancestor.
webster_full: DOWNWARD, DOWNWARDS, adv. From a higher place to a lower; in a descending course; as, to tend, move, roll, look, or fall downward.
2. In a course of lineal descent from an ancestor.
3. In a course of successive time.
scriptures: And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward:
Ecc 3:21
Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?
Eze 8:2

Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber.
And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall yet again take root downward, and bear fruit upward.
corruption_summary: Growth is measured by what is visible above ground, and Isaiah's promise puts the root work first — downward before upward.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 37:31 states an order that cannot be reversed: shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward. The visible fruit is the second clause and the invisible rooting is the first, and the sequence is not decorative. A remnant recovering from siege is promised underground work before public results — which is a mercy, since root growth is precisely what a devastated people can do while nothing shows.

The same order governs individual recovery. Seasons in which nothing appears to be happening are not necessarily wasted; they may be the downward half of the promise. What eventually shows above ground is limited by what was put down beneath it, and no amount of attention to the fruit clause substitutes for the root clause.
roots_summary: Hebrew mattah (H4295), downward, beneath; maalah (H4605), upward — the pair in Isaiah 37:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew mattah (H4295) — downward, beneath; Isaiah 37:31, Ecclesiastes 3:21, Deuteronomy 28:43.
Hebrew maalah (H4605) — upward, above; the companion in Isaiah 37:31, bear fruit upward.
Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — root; the verb form in take root downward.
usage: “Take root downward, and bear fruit upward” — an order that cannot be reversed.
“The spirit of the beast that goeth downward” — Ecclesiastes' hard question.
“From his loins even downward… the appearance of fire” — Ezekiel's vision.

pos: adj. (full of uproar; rendering Hebrew shaon)
etymology: From Latin tumultus, an uproar. Tumultuous describes noise with a crowd in it — and Scripture applies it to nations and to sons of pride.
biblical_def: Tumultuous means full of uproar. Jeremiah announces judgment on Moab and “the crown of the head of the tumultuous ones” (Jer 48:45). Isaiah asks, “What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops? Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city” (Isa 22:1–2) — Jerusalem celebrating on its roofs when it should have been weeping. Psalm 65 says God stills “the tumult of the people” (Psa 65:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tumultuous as full of tumult; disorderly; turbulent; and conducted with tumult, agitated.
webster_full: TUMULTUOUS, a. Full of tumult; disorderly; turbulent.
2. Conducted with tumult; as a tumultuous rebellion.
3. Agitated; disturbed with conflicting passions.
4. Turbulent; violent; as tumultuous rage.
scriptures: Isa 22:2
Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.

They that fled stood under the shadow of Heshbon because of the force: but a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon, and shall devour the corner of Moab, and the crown of the head of the tumultuous ones.
Psa 65:7
Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people.
And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth:
corruption_summary: A loud, festive public mood is read as health, and Isaiah 22 describes a city celebrating on its rooftops in the year it should have mourned.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 22:12-13 is one of the sharpest indictments in the prophets, and its subject is the mismatch between the moment and the mood. In that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning… and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die. God called for mourning; the city threw a party. The tumultuous noise was not evidence of confidence but of refusal.

Psalm 65:7 is the answer to every roar: which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people. Sea-noise and crowd-noise are set in one sentence as things only God quiets. A believer who has learned to read the tumult of a nation the way he reads weather — real, loud, and entirely under God's hand — has gained something worth more than any political certainty.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaon (H7588), roar, uproar; hamon (H1995), multitude, noise; homiyah (H1993), tumultuous, in Isaiah 22:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaon (H7588) — roar, tumult; Jeremiah 48:45, Isaiah 17:12, Psalm 65:7.
Hebrew homiyah (H1993) — noisy, tumultuous; Isaiah 22:2, a tumultuous city.
Hebrew hamon (H1995) — multitude, noise; the companion word throughout.
usage: “A tumultuous city, a joyous city” — the mood that did not match the hour.
“The Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping… and behold joy and gladness” — the mismatch named.
“Stilleth… the tumult of the people” — crowd-noise read as weather.
